title: Arguments & Entailment
goal: Decide whether an argument is valid, pick every formula a premise entails (Quiz 2 Q5(b) style), write a short entailment proof, reason about requirements, and read `∀`/`∃` in the right order.
magic: Valid argument = no row has all premises T and the conclusion F.
Only premise-rows count. One bad premise-row = `⊭`.
Specs: unsatisfiable = can't build; entailed = always holds; entailed by the rest = redundant.

blocks.title: 💡 Learn it, one idea at a time
An argument is valid when true premises force a true conclusion
blocks.summary: Premises + conclusion. Valid = whenever every premise is T, the conclusion is T too.
blocks.picture: A detective says: "If the butler did it, there's mud on his boots. There's no mud on his boots. So the butler didn't do it." If you believe both clues, you **must** believe the conclusion. That's a valid argument.
blocks.official: An **argument** is a set of declarative sentences, the **premises**, plus one sentence, the **conclusion** (Week 2, slide 15). It is **valid** if the conclusion is true **whenever all the premises are true** (slide 16). Rows where some premise is false don't matter. Also said as: the conclusion *logically follows from* / is a *logical consequence of* the premises; the premises *entail* the conclusion.

watch.q: "If the alarm rings, the dog barks. If the dog barks, the neighbour wakes up. The alarm rings. So the neighbour wakes up." Valid?
steps: Letters: `a` = the alarm rings, `d` = the dog barks, `n` = the neighbour wakes up.
Premises: `a ⇒ d`, `d ⇒ n`, `a`. Conclusion: `n`.
Assume every premise is T. From `a` = T and `a ⇒ d`: `d` = T.
From `d` = T and `d ⇒ n`: `n` = T. The conclusion is forced.
watch.answer: **Valid.** Written `a ⇒ d, d ⇒ n, a ⊨ n`.

tries.q: "If it's a holiday, the office is closed. The office is closed. So it's a holiday." Valid?
tries.a: **Invalid.** Counter-row: `h = F, c = T`: both premises T, conclusion F.
tries.why: The office can be closed for another reason (a strike, a weekend). This mistake has a name: *affirming the consequent*.
tries.letters: `h` = it's a holiday · `c` = the office is closed

tries.q: "The key is in my bag or my coat. It's not in my bag. So it's in my coat." Valid?
tries.why: With `b ∨ c` = T and `¬b` = T, `b` is F, so `c` must be T.
tries.letters: `b` = in my bag · `c` = in my coat

tries.q: "If the tests pass, we deploy. We didn't deploy. So the tests didn't pass." Valid?
tries.why: If the tests had passed (`t` = T), `t ⇒ d` would force `d` = T. But `d` = F. So `t` = F.

tries.q: "If you're a student, you get a discount. You're not a student. So you don't get a discount." Valid?
tries.why: Non-students might get a discount too (seniors). The premises say nothing about non-students. This mistake is *denying the antecedent*.
tries.letters: `s` = you're a student · `d` = you get a discount

trap.tempting: The conclusion is true in real life, so the argument is valid.
trap.correct: Validity is about the **form**: in every row where all premises are T, is the conclusion T? A true conclusion can come from an invalid argument.
trap.test: Look for a row with all premises T and the conclusion F. If one exists, it's invalid, whatever happens in real life.

blocks.magic: Valid = no row has all premises T and the conclusion F.

blocks.title: The truth-table test, and the one counter-row
blocks.summary: Mark only the rows where all premises are T. Check the conclusion there. One bad row = invalid.
blocks.picture: Checking a bouncer's rule: you only look at the people who were **let in**. If even one of them has no ticket, the rule failed.
blocks.official: `φ₁, …, φₙ ⊨ φ` means: in **every row** of the truth table where `φ₁, …, φₙ` are all T, `φ` is T too (Week 2, slide 18). The slides mark only the T entries (blank = F) to keep the table readable (slide 19). If the argument is invalid, **one** row with all premises T and the conclusion F proves it: `⊭` (slide 20).

watch.q: Is `p ⇒ q, r ⇒ q, q ⊨ p ∨ r`?
steps: Rows where all three premises are T: `q` must be T, and then `p ⇒ q` and `r ⇒ q` are T whatever `p`, `r` are.
So the premise-rows are the 4 rows with `q = T`.
Check the conclusion `p ∨ r` in each: row `p = F, q = T, r = F` gives F.
watch.answer: **Not entailed:** `p ⇒ q, r ⇒ q, q ⊭ p ∨ r`. Counter-row: `p = F, q = T, r = F`.

tries.q: Is `¬p ⇒ q, ¬q ⊨ p`?
tries.why: Premise-rows: `¬q` forces `q = F`. Then `¬p ⇒ F` needs `¬p` = F, so `p = T`. The only premise-row has `p = T`.

tries.q: Is `p ⇒ (q ∨ r), p, ¬q ⊨ r`?
tries.why: Premise-rows: `p = T`, `q = F`, and then `q ∨ r` must be T, so `r = T`. Conclusion `r` = T.

tries.q: Is `p ∨ q, q ∨ r ⊨ p ∨ r`? If not, give a counter-row.
tries.a: **No.** Counter-row: `p = F, q = T, r = F`.
tries.why: `q` = T makes both premises T on its own, and then `p`, `r` can both be F.

tries.q: Is `p ⇔ q, q ⇔ r ⊨ p ⇔ r`?
tries.why: Premise-rows: `p` matches `q` and `q` matches `r`, so all three match (FFF or TTT). Then `p ⇔ r` is T.

trap.tempting: Look at every row, including rows where a premise is false.
trap.correct: Rows with **any** false premise are ignored. Only the all-premises-T rows count.
trap.test: Step 1: find the premise-rows. Step 2: check the conclusion only there.

blocks.magic: Only premise-rows count. One premise-row with a false conclusion = `⊭`.

blocks.title: Which formulas are entailed? (the Quiz 2 Q5(b) method)
blocks.summary: Find the premise's rows once, then test each option only on those rows.
blocks.picture: A filter: the premise throws away every "world" where it's false. An option is entailed if it is true in **every** world that survived.
blocks.official: Given premise(s) and a list of candidate formulas: (1) list **all** rows that make the premise(s) true; (2) a candidate is entailed exactly when it is T in **every one** of those rows. One premise-row where the candidate is F rules it out. Candidates equivalent to the premise are always entailed.

watch.q: Which of these are entailed by `(p ⇔ q) ∧ ¬r`? (1) `¬r` (2) `p ⇒ q` (3) `p` (4) `q ∨ r` (5) `p ⊕ q`
steps: Premise-rows: `¬r` → `r = F`. `p ⇔ q` → `p`, `q` match. So: `p = F, q = F, r = F` and `p = T, q = T, r = F`.
(1) `¬r`: T in both ✅.
(3) `p`: F in the first row ❌.
(4) `q ∨ r`: F in the first row ❌.
(5) `p ⊕ q`: F in both rows ❌.

tries.q: Which are entailed by `p ∧ (q ∨ r)`?
tries.why: Premise-rows: TFT, TTF, TTT. (1) `p` is T in all. (3) `q ∨ r` is T in all. (4) `¬q ⇒ r` is the same as `q ∨ r`. (2) `q` fails at TFT; (5) `q ∧ r` fails at TFT and TTF.

tries.q: Which are entailed by `¬(p ∨ q) ∨ r`?
tries.why: Premise-rows: FFF, FFT, FTT, TFT, TTT. (1) is the same formula as the premise (`¬X ∨ r` = `X ⇒ r`). (3) every premise-row with `p = T` has `r = T`. (5) every premise-row with `q = T` has `r = T`. (2) `r` fails at FFF; (4) `¬q` fails at FTT.

tries.q: Which are entailed by `a ∧ ¬b`?
tries.why: Only one premise-row: `a = T, b = F`. Evaluate each option there: (1) `a ∨ b` = T. (2) `b ⇒ a` = F ⇒ T = T. (3) `a ⇔ b` = F. (4) `¬(a ⇒ b)` = ¬(T ⇒ F) = T.

trap.tempting: An option is entailed if it's true in **some** premise-row.
trap.correct: It must be true in **every** premise-row. One premise-row where it's F rules it out.
trap.test: Write the premise-rows in a mini-table. For each option, hunt for a single F.

blocks.magic: List the premise-rows once. Entailed = T in all of them.

blocks.title: Entailment is a valid implication (and how to prove one)
blocks.summary: `φ₁, …, φₙ ⊨ ψ` exactly when `(φ₁ ∧ … ∧ φₙ) ⇒ ψ` is valid. Also `φ ≡ ψ` exactly when `φ ⇔ ψ` is valid.
blocks.picture: "Given these clues, the answer must be X" is the same claim as "the rule *if all these clues then X* never fails".
blocks.official: **Theorem (Week 2, slide 27).** These are all the same: `φ₁, …, φₙ ⊨ ψ` · `⊨ (φ₁ ∧ … ∧ φₙ) ⇒ ψ` · `⊨ φ₁ ⇒ (φ₂ ⇒ … (φₙ ⇒ ψ)…)`. **Theorem.** `φ ≡ ψ` if and only if `⊨ φ ⇔ ψ`. To **prove** an entailment in words: assume every premise is true, then show step by step that the conclusion must be true (or check every premise-row).

watch.q: Prove that `r` follows logically from `p ∨ q`, `p ⇒ r` and `q ⇒ r`.
steps: Assume all three premises are true.
From `p ∨ q`, at least one of `p`, `q` is true. Split into cases.
Case `p` true: `p ⇒ r` is true, so `r` is true.
Case `q` true: `q ⇒ r` is true, so `r` is true.
In every case `r` is true.
watch.answer: So `p ∨ q, p ⇒ r, q ⇒ r ⊨ r`. (This is proof by cases in miniature.)

tries.q: Rewrite `a, a ⇒ b ⊨ b` as a single valid formula.
tries.why: Premises joined with `∧` on the left of `⇒`, conclusion on the right.

tries.q: Rewrite `a, a ⇒ b ⊨ b` using only `⇒` (the nested form).
tries.why: Each premise becomes one more `⇒` layer, in order.

tries.q: You want to show `x ⇒ y ≡ ¬y ⇒ ¬x`. Which single formula should be valid?
tries.why: `φ ≡ ψ` exactly when `⊨ φ ⇔ ψ`.

tries.q: Prove in words that `¬s` follows from `s ⇒ t`, `¬t ∨ u` and `¬u`.
tries.a: Assume all premises true. `¬u` means `u` is false. Then `¬t ∨ u` needs `¬t` true, so `t` is false. If `s` were true, `s ⇒ t` would make `t` true, which is impossible. So `s` is false, i.e. `¬s` is true.
tries.why: Chase what each premise forces, starting from the one that fixes a letter outright.

trap.tempting: `φ ⊨ ψ` and `φ ⇒ ψ` are the same kind of thing.
trap.correct: `φ ⇒ ψ` is a **formula** (true or false in each row). `φ ⊨ ψ` is a **claim about all rows**: it's true exactly when `φ ⇒ ψ` is valid.
trap.test: Ask: am I talking about one row (use `⇒`) or about every row (use `⊨`)?

blocks.magic: `⊨` = "`⇒` holds in every row". `≡` = "`⇔` holds in every row".

blocks.title: Reasoning about requirements: implementable, guaranteed, redundant
blocks.summary: Unsatisfiable spec = can't be built. Entailed property = always holds. Requirement entailed by the others = redundant.
blocks.picture: An app's feature list. If two features contradict, no one can build it. If a property follows from the list, every correct build has it. If one feature follows from the others, you can delete it from the list.
blocks.official: Write requirements as formulas `φ₁, …, φₙ` (Week 2, slide 21). (1) If `φ₁ ∧ … ∧ φₙ` is **unsatisfiable**, the requirements **cannot be implemented**. (2) If `φ₁, …, φₙ ⊨ ψ`, then **every** correct implementation makes `ψ` true. (3) If `φ₁, …, φₙ₋₁ ⊨ φₙ`, then `φₙ` is **redundant**. (The lecture's burglar-alarm example is Problem set 2, Q6.)

watch.q: A door system: (R1) the door opens only if a valid card **and** a correct code are given; (R2) if a valid card and correct code are given, the door opens; (R3) when the alarm is armed, the door never opens. Does every correct system satisfy: *"when armed, a valid card plus a correct code is never given"*?
steps: Letters: `o` = door opens, `c` = valid card, `k` = correct code, `a` = alarm armed.
Assume R1–R3 true and `a` = T. R3 → `o` = F.
R2's contrapositive: `¬o ⇒ ¬(c ∧ k)`. So `c ∧ k` = F. The claim holds.
watch.answer: **Yes:** `R1, R2, R3 ⊨ a ⇒ ¬(c ∧ k)`. (A real spec bug: while armed, the system can never accept a valid card and code.)

tries.q: Same door spec. Is R1 redundant, i.e. do R2 and R3 alone entail `o ⇒ (c ∧ k)`?
tries.a: **No, not redundant.** Counter-row: `o = T, c = F, k = F, a = F`.
tries.why: R2 is true (its left side is F) and R3 is true (`a` = F), but R1 is false: the door opened with no card.
tries.letters: `o` = opens · `c` = valid card · `k` = correct code · `a` = armed

tries.q: Someone adds R4: "the door opens only if a valid card is given" (`o ⇒ c`). Is R4 redundant given R1?
tries.why: If the door opens, R1 gives `c ∧ k`, and so `c`. R4 adds nothing.

tries.q: A lamp spec: "the lamp is on exactly when the door is open", "the door is open", "the lamp is off". Can it be implemented?
tries.why: `d` = T and `l ⇔ d` force `l` = T, but the third requirement says `l` = F.
tries.letters: `l` = the lamp is on · `d` = the door is open

tries.q: Does the door spec (R1–R3) guarantee `¬a`, i.e. the alarm is never armed?
tries.a: **No.** Counter-row: `a = T, o = F, c = F, k = F`. All of R1–R3 hold.
tries.why: An armed system with no card presented breaks nothing. Being armed is allowed.

trap.correct: Redundant means it is **entailed by the other requirements**: it's true in every system that meets them, so stating it adds nothing.
trap.test: Delete it from the list, then check: do the rest still entail it?

blocks.magic: Can't build = unsatisfiable. Always holds = entailed. Redundant = entailed by the others.

blocks.title: Liars and truth-tellers: `person ⇔ what they said`
blocks.summary: A truth-teller's statement is true; a liar's is false. So each speaker gives `X ⇔ statement`.
blocks.picture: On an island, some people always tell the truth and some always lie. You can't see who is who, but every sentence they say is a clue.
blocks.official: Let the letter `X` mean "X is a truth-teller". If `X` says `S`, then `X` is a truth-teller exactly when `S` is true: add the formula **`X ⇔ S`**. "`Y` is a liar" is `¬Y`. Solve the `∧` of all these formulas; each model is a possible world. (Problem set 2, Q6(b) is a puzzle of this kind.)

watch.q: Ava says: "At least one of us two is a liar." What are Ava and Ben?
steps: Formula: `A ⇔ (¬A ∨ ¬B)`.
Try `A` = F: then `¬A ∨ ¬B` = T, so the right side is T but the left is F. ❌
So `A` = T. The right side must be T: `¬A ∨ ¬B` = F ∨ ¬B, so `B` = F.
Check: Ava (truth-teller) says one of them lies: Ben does ✅.
watch.answer: **Ava is a truth-teller, Ben is a liar.**

tries.q: Cal says: "Dee and I are both truth-tellers." Dee says: "Cal is a liar." What are they?
tries.a: **Cal is a liar, Dee is a truth-teller.**
tries.why: Formulas: `C ⇔ (C ∧ D)` and `D ⇔ ¬C`. If `C` = T, the first needs `D` = T but the second needs `D` = F. So `C` = F; then `D ⇔ T` gives `D` = T.

tries.q: Eli: "Fay is a liar." Fay: "Eli and Gus are the same type." Gus: "Eli is a liar." Who is what?
tries.a: **Eli is a truth-teller; Fay and Gus are liars.**
tries.why: Formulas: `E ⇔ ¬F`, `F ⇔ (E ⇔ G)`, `G ⇔ ¬E`. Only `E = T, F = F, G = F` satisfies all three. Check Fay: `E ⇔ G` = T ⇔ F = F, and Fay is a liar ✅.

tries.q: Nia says: "I am a liar." What is Nia?
tries.a: **Impossible:** no one on the island can say that.
tries.why: The formula is `N ⇔ ¬N`, which is unsatisfiable. A truth-teller would be lying, and a liar would be telling the truth.

trap.tempting: Translate "Y is a liar" as `Y ⇒ ¬Y` or leave the speaker out.
trap.correct: Every statement gets wrapped as **`Speaker ⇔ (what they said)`**. "Y is a liar" is just `¬Y`.
trap.test: Count: one `⇔` formula per sentence spoken.

blocks.magic: Speaker `⇔` statement. Then find the models.

blocks.title: For all, there exists, and why the order matters
blocks.summary: `∀` = for all, `∃` = there exists. Swapping `∀x ∃y` to `∃y ∀x` can change the meaning.
blocks.picture: "Every student has a favourite song" (each can pick a different one) is not the same as "There's one song that is every student's favourite".
blocks.official: `∀` means **for all**; `∃` means **there exist(s)** (Week 2, slide 28, e.g. Goldbach: `∀n ∈ 2ℕ (n > 2 ⇒ ∃p, q ∈ ℕ (p, q ∈ Primes ∧ n = p + q))`). **Order matters** (slides 29–30): `∃y ∀x P(x, y) ⇒ ∀x ∃y P(x, y)` is always true, but `∀x ∃y P(x, y) ⇒ ∃y ∀x P(x, y)` is not. Example: `∀x ∈ ℤ (∃y ∈ ℤ (y ≤ x))` is true, but `∃y ∈ ℤ (∀x ∈ ℤ (y ≤ x))` is false. Over ℕ the second one is true (`y = 0`). Also useful: `¬∀x P ≡ ∃x ¬P` and `¬∃x P ≡ ∀x ¬P`.

watch.q: Domain `{1, 2, 3}`. True or false: (i) `∀x ∃y (x + y = 4)`, (ii) `∃y ∀x (x + y = 4)`.
steps: (i) For each `x`, can we find a `y`? `x = 1 → y = 3`, `x = 2 → y = 2`, `x = 3 → y = 1`. ✅
(ii) Is there ONE `y` that works for every `x`? `y = 3` fails for `x = 2`; `y = 2` fails for `x = 1`; `y = 1` fails for `x = 1`. ❌
watch.answer: **(i) true, (ii) false.** With `∀x ∃y`, `y` may depend on `x`; with `∃y ∀x`, one `y` must fit all.

tries.q: True or false over ℕ: `∀x ∃y (y > x)`.
tries.why: Given any `x`, take `y = x + 1`.

check.expr: all(any(y > x for y in range(0, 102)) for x in range(0, 100))

tries.q: True or false over ℕ: `∃y ∀x (y > x)`.
tries.why: Any candidate `y` fails for `x = y`. No natural number is bigger than all of them.

tries.q: True or false over `{0, 1, 2}`: `∃y ∀x (x · y = 0)`.
tries.why: One `y` must work for every `x`: `y = 0` makes every product 0.

check.expr: any(all(x*y == 0 for x in [0,1,2]) for y in [0,1,2])

tries.q: Write "every user has a password" and "some password is used by every user" with `Has(u, p)`. Which implies which?
tries.a: "Every user has a password": `∀u ∃p Has(u, p)`. "Some password is used by every user": `∃p ∀u Has(u, p)`. The second implies the first, not the other way round.
tries.why: `∃p ∀u` ⇒ `∀u ∃p` is always true (slide 29). The reverse fails when users have different passwords.

tries.q: Negate `∀x ∈ ℤ (x² ≥ 0)` so that `¬` sits right next to the inner statement. Is the result true?
tries.a: `∃x ∈ ℤ (x² < 0)`. **False**, because the original is true.

check.expr: not any(x*x < 0 for x in range(-50, 51))

trap.correct: In `∀x ∃y`, `y` can be different for each `x`. In `∃y ∀x`, one single `y` must work for **all** `x`.
trap.test: Try to name ONE `y` up front. If you can't, `∃y ∀x` is false.

blocks.magic: `∃y ∀x` ⇒ `∀x ∃y`, never the other way round in general.

items.q: What does `a, b ⊨ c` say in words?
items.a: **Whenever `a` and `b` are both true, `c` is true.**
items.why: The premises are left of `⊨`; the conclusion is on the right.

items.q: Is `p ∧ q ⊨ p`?
items.why: Premise-row: `p = T, q = T`. `p` is T there.

items.q: Is `p ⊨ p ∧ q`?
items.why: The premise says nothing about `q`.

items.q: Is `q ⊨ p ∨ q`?
items.why: If `q` is T, then `p ∨ q` is T.

items.q: "Either the bus is late or I overslept. I didn't oversleep. So the bus is late." Valid?
items.why: `b ∨ o, ¬o ⊨ b`: with `o` = F, `b` must be T.
items.letters: `b` = the bus is late · `o` = I overslept

items.q: True or false over `{1, 2}`: `∀x ∃y (x ≠ y)`.

check.expr: all(any(x != y for y in [1,2]) for x in [1,2])

items.q: Is `p ⇒ q, q ⇒ p ⊨ p ⇔ q`?
items.why: `p ⇔ q` is exactly `(p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ p)`.

items.q: Is `p ⇒ q, ¬p ⊨ ¬q`? If not, a counter-row.
items.why: Both premises T, conclusion `¬q` = F. (Denying the antecedent.)

items.q: Is `(a ∧ b) ⇒ c, a, ¬c ⊨ ¬b`?
items.why: With `a` = T and `c` = F, `(a ∧ b) ⇒ c` needs `a ∧ b` = F, so `b` = F.

items.q: `φ ⊨ ψ` and `ψ ⊨ φ` are both true. What can you say?
items.why: They have the same premise-rows in both directions, so they agree in every row.

items.q: Is `p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ r ⊨ q ∨ r`?
items.why: If `p` = T, `¬p ∨ r` forces `r` = T. If `p` = F, `p ∨ q` forces `q` = T. Either way `q ∨ r` = T.

items.q: Specs `s ⇒ l` and `l ⇒ ¬s`. Can they be implemented? What must be true in every implementation?
items.a: **Yes, implementable** (e.g. all false). Every implementation has **`¬s`**.
items.why: If `s` = T: `l` = T, then `¬s` = T. Contradiction. So `s` = F in every model.

items.q: True or false: `∀x ∈ ℤ ∃y ∈ ℤ (x + y = 0)`, and `∃y ∈ ℤ ∀x ∈ ℤ (x + y = 0)`.
items.why: First: `y = −x`. Second: one `y` can't cancel every `x` (try `x = 0` and `x = 1`).

blocks.sub: Quiz 2 is a variation of Problem set 2, Q5(b): *which formulas are entailed by …?* Plus one Q5(a)-style written proof. All premises here are original.

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `(p ⇒ q) ∧ ¬q`?
items.why: Premise-rows: `¬q` → `q = F`; `p ⇒ F` → `p = F`. One row: `p = F, q = F` (with `r` free). (1) `¬p` ✅. (2) `p ⇒ r` ✅ (F ⇒ …). (3) `r` ❌ (can be F). (4) `¬p ∧ ¬q` ✅. (5) `q ∨ r` ❌ when `r = F`.

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `(A ⊕ B) ∧ ¬C`?
items.why: Premise-rows (`A B C`): FTF and TFF. (1) `¬C` ✅. (2) `A ∨ B` ✅. (3) `A` ❌ at FTF. (4) `A ⇔ ¬B` ✅ (that's another way to write `A ⊕ B`). (5) `B ⇒ C` ❌ at FTF (T ⇒ F).

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `(P ⇔ Q) ∨ R`?
items.why: Premise-rows: the 4 rows with `P = Q`, plus the rows with `R = T`: FFF, FFT, FTT, TFT, TTF, TTT. (1) `R` ❌ at FFF. (2) `P ⇒ Q` ❌ at TFT. (3) `(P ⊕ Q) ⇒ R` ✅ (the same formula written differently). (4) `P ∨ Q ∨ R` ❌ at FFF.

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `P ⇒ (Q ∧ R)`?
items.why: Premise-rows (`P Q R`): the four `P = F` rows plus TTT. (1) `¬P ∨ R` ✅ (the only `P = T` row has `R = T`). (2) `Q ⇒ P` ❌ at FTF. (3) `P ⇒ Q` ✅. (4) `R` ❌ at FFF. (5) `¬(P ∧ ¬R)` ✅ (same as (1)).

items.q: Which are logically entailed by `(x ∧ ¬y) ⊕ z`?
items.why: Premise-rows (`x y z`): TFF (left T, `z` F) plus the `z = T` rows where `x ∧ ¬y` is F: FFT, FTT, TTT. (1) `z` ❌ at TFF. (2) `x` ❌ at FFT. (3) `x ∨ z` ✅. (4) `¬y` ❌ at FTT.

items.q: Prove that `¬m` follows logically from `m ⇒ (n ∧ k)` and `¬k ∨ ¬n`.
items.a: Assume both premises. Suppose `m` were true. Then `m ⇒ (n ∧ k)` gives `n` and `k` both true. But then `¬k ∨ ¬n` is F ∨ F = false, contradicting the second premise. So `m` is false: `¬m` holds.
items.why: A written proof: assume the premises, then show the conclusion is forced (here by ruling out `m` = T).

items.q: The premises `p` and `¬p` entail every formula, even `q`. Why?
items.a: **There is no row where both premises are T**, so there's no row that could break the entailment.
items.why: `⊨` only looks at premise-rows. With none, every conclusion passes. (Unsatisfiable requirements "prove" anything, which is why they're useless.)

items.q: Is `∀x ∃y P(x, y) ⇒ ∃y ∀x P(x, y)` a tautology? Give a counterexample if not.
items.a: **No.** Domain `{1, 2}`, `P(x, y)` = "`x = y`": every `x` equals some `y`, but no single `y` equals both `x`s.
items.why: `∀x ∃y` lets `y` depend on `x`; `∃y ∀x` doesn't (Week 2, slide 29).

check.expr: all(any(x == y for y in [1,2]) for x in [1,2]) and not any(all(x == y for x in [1,2]) for y in [1,2])

items.q: Door spec R1–R3 from Idea 5. The team adds R5: "when armed, a valid card plus correct code still opens the door": `(a ∧ c ∧ k) ⇒ o`. Is the new spec implementable? What does it now force?
items.a: **Still implementable**, but now every implementation has **`¬(a ∧ c ∧ k)`**: armed + valid card + correct code must never happen at all.
items.why: R3 gives `a ⇒ ¬o`; R5 then forces `a ∧ c ∧ k` to be false. The spec is satisfiable (e.g. everything F) but it quietly bans a real situation.

items.q: Three islanders. Ivy: "Jo and Kit are different types." Jo: "At least one of Ivy and Kit is a liar." Kit: "Exactly one of us three is a truth-teller." Who is what?
items.a: **Ivy and Jo are truth-tellers; Kit is a liar.**
items.why: Split on Kit. If Kit tells the truth, Ivy and Jo are liars; but then Ivy's claim "Jo (liar) and Kit (truth-teller) differ" is true, and a liar can't say something true ❌. So Kit is a liar. Then Jo's claim is true (Kit lies), so Jo is a truth-teller. Ivy's claim (Jo T, Kit F: different) is true, so Ivy is a truth-teller. Check Kit: there are 2 truth-tellers, so "exactly one" is false ✅.

items.q: `φ ⊨ ψ` holds. Must `¬ψ ⊨ ¬φ` hold too?
items.why: `φ ⊨ ψ` means `φ ⇒ ψ` is valid. Its contrapositive `¬ψ ⇒ ¬φ` is equivalent, so it's valid too.

items.q: Is `a ⇒ b, b ⊨ a`?
Which are entailed by `x ∧ (y ⇒ z)`? (1) `x` (2) `z` (3) `¬z ⇒ ¬y` (4) `y`
Write `p, q ⊨ r` as one valid formula.
Over `{1, 2, 3}`: is `∃y ∀x (x ≤ y)` true?

check.expr: any(all(x <= y for x in [1,2,3]) for y in [1,2,3])

lines: Argument = premises + conclusion. Valid (`⊨`) = conclusion T in every row where all premises are T.
Invalid? Show ONE counter-row: premises all T, conclusion F.
Picking entailed options: list the premise-rows once, test each option on all of them.
`⊨` ↔ a valid `⇒`; `≡` ↔ a valid `⇔`. A written proof: assume the premises, force the conclusion.
Requirements: unsatisfiable → can't implement; entailed → guaranteed; entailed by the others → redundant.
Liars/truth-tellers: add `X ⇔ (what X said)` for each speaker.
`∀x ∃y`: `y` may depend on `x`. `∃y ∀x`: one `y` for all `x`. Negation: `¬∀ = ∃¬`, `¬∃ = ∀¬`.
